props.title: Who's That Knocking at My Door

sections.content: Martin Scorsese's debut feature Who's That Knocking at My Door established many of his career-long preoccupations: Catholic guilt, masculine identity in crisis, and the streets of New York City. Shot in black and white over several years while Scorsese was still at NYU, the film stars Harvey Keitel in his first role as J.R., a young Italian-American Catholic struggling to reconcile his religious beliefs with his relationship with a modern woman (Zina Bethune). The raw energy and experimental editing techniques, particularly in the sex scene montages, showed clear influence from the French New Wave, especially Breathless (1960) and Band of Outsiders (1964).

sections.content: The film's production history reveals Scorsese's early determination. Originally titled "I Call First," it began as his student thesis film before expanding into a feature over several years. The influence of John Cassavetes' Shadows (1959) is evident in its documentary-like street scenes and raw emotional authenticity. The film's exploration of male-female relationships and sexual politics would become recurring themes in Scorsese's work, reaching fuller expression in Taxi Driver (1976) and Raging Bull (1980).

The religious imagery and themes of Catholic guilt that permeate Who's That Knocking at My Door would become signature elements of Scorsese's filmography, culminating in The Last Temptation of Christ (1988) and Silence (2016). The film's innovative editing techniques, particularly in the dream sequences and fantasy montages, show the influence of experimental filmmakers like Kenneth Anger and Stan Brakhage, while presaging Scorsese's later stylistic flourishes. SUBHEAD: Early American Independent Cinema Context

The film emerged during a crucial period in American independent cinema, alongside works like Easy Rider (1969) and Faces (1968). Its raw examination of urban life and cultural identity helped pave the way for the New Hollywood movement of the 1970s. The film's authentic portrayal of Italian-American life in New York City would influence later works like Saturday Night Fever (1977) and Prince of the City (1981).
